title: Fundamental Attribution Error
description: We over-attribute others’ negative behavior to their character, while excusing our own identical behavior due to circumstances.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We over-attribute others’ negative behavior to their character, while excusing our own identical behavior due to circumstances.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A colleague snaps at you: “They’re such a rude person.” The same morning, you snapped at someone because you slept badly—and you label your own behavior as “just having a rough day.”
A driver cuts you off: “Idiot.” When you cut someone off, it’s because you’re late and usually a safe driver.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Instant character judgments after single negative interactions.
Forgiving yourself quickly, holding grudges against others.
Using different vocabulary for the same action (“I was assertive; they were aggressive”).

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You hear yourself thinking “That’s just how they are” after one incident.
You never ask “What might have caused that?” when it’s someone else’s mistake.
In relationships, you catalog their faults as permanent traits while seeing yours as situational.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Perceptually, the person is the focus of your attention, while their situation is background. For yourself, you’re acutely aware of your own context.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When judging another’s behavior, deliberately ask: “What situational pressures could have caused this?”
Pretend you are their defense lawyer for 60 seconds before concluding.
Track your own attribution vocabulary: notice when you say “they are” vs “they did.”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you’re immune because you know about it. The bias operates automatically; it needs active countering.
Over-correcting and making endless excuses for genuinely bad behavior.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A project manager misses a deadline. The team immediately grumbles about her being disorganized. Weeks later, they learn her parent was hospitalized that week. The judgment was instant; the context came far too late.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: When someone acts badly, assume their day is harder than yours—until proven otherwise.
